documents: Gong, Wang & Geng (2024) Geophysical Prospecting 72:20-34, published paper (PDF)

entry.evidence: Therefore, it is very important to separate SDWs from seismic records on a rugged surface.

steps.action: The authors pose the problem of separating scattered direct waves (SDWs), generated by a rugged surface and dominating land reflection records, from reflections.
steps.quote: Therefore, it is very important to separate SDWs from seismic records on a rugged surface.

steps.action: The authors review traditional random and coherent noise suppression methods (predictive filtering, sparse transforms, rank reduction, F–K, tau-p, scattered-noise filters) and cite their limits for SDWs.
steps.quote: Therefore, so far it is difficult to build an accurate model to describe signal or noise for the suppressing of SDWs.

steps.action: The authors build a convolutional autoencoder (three convolutional and three deconvolutional layers, 5x5 kernels, ReLU with identity output) trained by residual learning with a Frobenius-norm loss and the Adam optimizer to predict DWs and SDWs.
steps.quote: The entire network is composed of one input layer, three convolutional layers and three deconvolutional layers.

steps.action: The authors design the training scheme: paired velocity models with the same rugged surface, a layered model for input and a uniform half-space for SDW-only labels.
steps.quote: In the numerical experiments, we design a pair of two velocity models with the same rugged surface

steps.action: The authors randomly perturb surface elevation within 100 m to generate 5000 model pairs and simulate elastic shot gathers with the spectral element method (10 Hz Ricker, 201 receivers).
steps.quote: we generate 5000 pairs of velocity models like Figure 3 for seismic wave forward modelling

steps.action: The authors train the CAE in TensorFlow on 80% of the synthetic shot gathers (learning rate 0.001, 5000 epochs).
steps.quote: we use 80% of the synthetic shot gathers as the training dataset while the rest as the testing dataset

steps.action: The authors compare training and held-out testing loss curves and find they coincide, indicating no overfitting.
steps.quote: indicating that the network is not over-fitted and has generalization ability

steps.action: For the one-reflector model, the authors compare CAE-denoised shot gathers, zero-offset profiles and stacked profiles with the input, with label subtraction (ground truth) and with F–K filtering.
steps.quote: the zero-offset profiles after suppressing DWs and SDWs by F–K filtering and subtracting the label from the input of the trained network

steps.action: The authors apply the approach to a second synthetic model with four reflectors.
steps.quote: Further, we carry out a numerical experiment on the model with four reflectors shown in Figure 8.

steps.action: The authors compare shot gathers, zero-offset and stacked profiles of the four-reflector model and judge CAE reflections stronger than F–K results.
steps.quote: the P-wave reflections processed by the trained CAE network are stronger than those processed by F–K filtering.

steps.action: The authors apply the approach to a modified Marmousi2 model with a homogeneous rugged top layer containing three scattering bodies.
steps.quote: For more complex model experiments, we further use a modified Marmousi2 model

steps.action: The authors compare Marmousi2 shot gathers and profiles and find F–K leaves weaker reflections and stronger residual direct waves than the CAE.
steps.quote: the filtered reflections in Figure 15c are not as obvious as those denoised by the CAE network in Figure 15b.

steps.action: The authors train a plain CNN with the same number of layers on the same data and configuration as an alternative network.
steps.quote: we build a convolutional neural network (CNN) with the same number of layers for comparison.

steps.action: The authors compare loss curves, training time and Marmousi2 denoising of the CAE and CNN, and find similar denoising at lower training cost for the CAE.
steps.quote: the CAE network takes only 130 minutes on an 8-core GPU node for network training, while the CNN takes 160 minutes.

steps.action: The authors attribute residual second-order scattered waves in the profiles to the label design, which cannot simulate scattering of reflections without a known subsurface model, rather than to the network.
steps.quote: Due to this, we see that there are second-order scattered waves in the zero-offset and stacked profiles.

steps.action: The authors examine testing loss shot by shot for 140 Marmousi2 shot gathers and find it varies across gathers.
steps.quote: We find that the values of testing loss are different from each shot gather.

steps.action: The authors propose more surface-elevation models for training diversity and, for real data, labels combining modelled SDWs with SDWs separated by other methods.
steps.quote: we should generate more models of surface elevation to expand the diversity of the training data.

steps.action: The authors conclude that the CAE approach has good potential for suppressing complex SDWs, on the evidence of three synthetic models.
steps.quote: Numerical examples of the three different models prove that the proposed approach has good potential for suppressing the complex scattered direct waves

tree.answer: Scattered direct waves from rugged surfaces, taken as known strong coherent noise
Visible in synthetic shot gathers; separation from reflections is the difficulty
Build a method that separates SDWs from reflections
Rival methods only: F–K filtering and a plain CNN; no rival hypotheses
No distinct quantitative predictions; visual comparison of profiles
Conditions set computationally with randomly perturbed rugged surfaces
Held-out loss, three models, label reference, F–K and CNN baselines; per-shot loss varies
Method has good potential on synthetic data

end.claim: A convolutional autoencoder trained on paired rugged-surface and uniform half-space synthetics can separate direct and scattered direct waves from synthetic reflection records better than F–K filtering.

decisive_move.sentence: Pairing each layered model with a uniform half-space under the same rugged surface supplies SDW-only labels, without which supervised training would be impossible.

gates.evidence: Synthetic data were generated to train a method, not directed by a stated hypothesis. The claim faced held-out testing, a ground-truth label comparison and F–K and CNN baselines, but success was judged visually with no metric or threshold. Nothing is said to have been fixed in advance.

imports.item: Patch-size trade-off for denoising strong-energy noise (Levin & Nadler 2011)

novelty_claims.quote: its applications in suppressing SDWs, generated by a complex rugged surface, are scanty.
we propose an approach to using the convolutional autoencoder, a deep learning network, to intelligently separate scattered direct waves from seismic records on a rugged [...]

limits:
1. All tests are synthetic; no field data are processed, and the authors name real data as a major open challenge (p. 32).
2. No quantitative quality metric (for example SNR or error against the label) is reported for the denoised profiles; comparisons are visual, apart from loss curves and training time.
3. The paper does not say whether the network was retrained for the four-reflector and Marmousi2 models or the one-reflector network was applied to them. It also does not say how many model pairs those models used. Inference: separate training sets were simulated for each model, since paired label models are described for each.
4. F–K filter parameters are not given, so the baseline's tuning is unknown.
5. The "100 epochs of testing" procedure is not explained.
6. The CNN cost comparison rests on single training runs.
7. Data are available only on request; no code is released.
8. No review file was supplied, so the review history is unknown.
9. Sub-claims: the CAE is cheaper to train than a same-depth CNN with similar denoising (capability_characterized, one run). Second-order scattered waves from reflections remain unremoved (acknowledged limit, no status).

disagreements.target: Traditional denoising methods (predictive filtering, sparse transforms, rank reduction) applied to SDWs
disagreements.support: The authors argue from cited literature that SDWs overlap reflections in t-x and f-k domains and break linear-prediction and low-rank assumptions, and they show F–K filtering underperforming the CAE on synthetics.
disagreements.quote: SDWs are characterized by strong energy and complex wave field characteristics in seismic records, which make traditional denoising methods difficult to work.

disagreements.target: Treating SDWs as conventional surface waves or ground roll
disagreements.support: The authors argue from generation mechanism: SDWs come from a rugged surface, ground roll from near-surface layering; no test is offered.
disagreements.quote: Notably, SDWs are quite different from conventional surface waves or ground rolls.

alternatives_considered.alternatives: CNN with the same number of layers; fully connected network
alternatives_considered.reason: Local connections reduce parameters; encoding/decoding compresses data and lowers training cost

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Dividing data into small patches or increasing patch size
alternatives_considered.reason: Larger patches needed for strong-energy noise increase network parameters

alternatives_considered.chosen: Synthetic training data with SDW-only labels from uniform half-space models
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Field data with labels from traditional denoising methods
alternatives_considered.reason: Field data are limited and labels without SDWs are hard to obtain by traditional denoising

alternatives_considered.chosen: Identity activation in the output layer
alternatives_considered.reason: Separation of SDWs is a prediction problem
